title: Brake-drum forge with a salvaged blower
summary: A cast-iron brake drum (or a heavy steel wheel) makes the firepot, a steel pipe brings air up from below, and a salvaged blower drives a charcoal fire to forging heat. Set it on a steady stand at hip height, outdoors. With it you can bend, draw out and harden steel into hooks, hinges, nails, chisels, tongs and repair parts. The dangers are serious: burns, carbon monoxide, flying scale, fire spreading, and zinc fumes from galvanised steel, which must never go near the fire.

materials.item: Brake drum, cast iron, 25–40 cm across (car, van or light-truck rear drum), or a heavy steel wheel rim
Air pipe: plain steel pipe or tube 25–50 mm across, about 1 m, with a flange or bracket to fix it under the drum, a tee and a removable end cap. Not galvanised
Grate over the air hole: a piece of cast-iron grill grate, 5–6 mm steel plate drilled with 6–10 holes of 6–10 mm, or a few plain bolts laid across
Blower: an inflatable-decoration blower, a hair dryer on its cold setting, or a vacuum motor run on blow
Air control: a sliding steel gate in the pipe, or a cover that can partly block the blower intake
Charcoal crushed to 1–3 cm, dust sieved out (build_charcoal_retort)
Anvil: a heavy steel block, a length of rail or a sledgehammer head, fixed on a stump
Tongs or locking pliers, a 1–1.5 kg hammer, a bucket of water and a bucket of sand
Safety glasses, leather gloves and apron, cotton or wool clothes, ear protection
Hose or duct from blower to pipe (vacuum hose), long enough to keep the blower 1 m from the fire
Stand: steel legs, a wheel rim, an old grill frame or a stack of bricks, to hold the drum at 70–90 cm
Bolts M8–M12 with nuts, to fix the flange and legs
Clay and sand for a lining

steps.text: Get a brake drum: a rear drum from a car, van or light truck, cast iron, 10–25 kg. Clean off the brake dust.
steps.warn: Brake dust from older vehicles can contain asbestos. Don't blow or brush it: wet it, wipe with a damp rag, bag the rag, and wear a mask (safety_asbestos_check).

steps.text: Check every metal part that will sit in or near the fire: pipe, fittings, grate, bolts and stand. Reject anything galvanised (dull grey, crystal-patterned or white-crusted zinc coating) or zinc-plated (shiny silver or gold-tinted bolts).
steps.warn: Never heat galvanised steel. Its zinc gives off white fumes that cause metal-fume fever: chills, fever and aches for a day or two, worse each time. If zinc gets in the fire, step away upwind until the smoke clears.

steps.text: Make the grate: cover the drum's centre hole with drilled plate or a piece of cast-iron grate, or lay bolts across it. The holes together should add up to about the area of your air pipe.

Fit the air pipe under the centre hole using the drum's stud holes and a flange or a bracket bolted across. Run it down 20–30 cm to a tee: one branch goes to the blower, the bottom gets a removable cap so ash can drop out.
Build the stand so the drum's rim sits at 70–90 cm, about where your knuckles hang. Make it wide-footed and set it on bare ground or concrete.
steps.warn: A drum, pipe and stand weigh 20–40 kg. Lift with a second person, and make sure it can't tip: a falling forge scatters burning fuel.

steps.text: Optional lining: press a 2–5 cm layer of clay mixed with about the same amount of sand into the drum, shaped into a bowl round the grate. Let it dry for a day or two, then fire gently the first time so it doesn't crack.
Connect the blower to the side of the tee by hose or straight on, with a sliding gate or partial intake cover to control air. Keep the blower and its cord at least 1 m from the fire, out of the rain.
steps.warn: Mains blowers and cords near heat and water can kill. Keep cords off hot ground and away from the quench bucket, and use an RCD (GFCI) if you can.

steps.text: Set up outdoors on bare ground or concrete, 3 m from anything that burns, with nothing overhead. Under a roof only if it is high and open on at least two sides. Put the water and sand buckets within reach.
steps.warn: Never run a forge in a closed garage, shed or room. Charcoal fires make carbon monoxide without visible smoke (safety_carbon_monoxide).

steps.text: Light it: paper and kindling on the grate, a small heap of charcoal on top, light it, then add gentle air. Build the charcoal into a mound 10–15 cm deep over the air hole.

Heat a piece of plain steel in the middle of the mound, covered with charcoal, not on top and not right down in the air blast. Use only as much air as it takes to bring it to orange or yellow in a few minutes.
steps.warn: White sparks shooting off the steel mean it is burning away: pull it out and cut back the air.

steps.text: Work it: hold it with tongs, hammer on the anvil, and put it back in the fire before it drops below a dull red. Lay hot pieces in one marked place to cool.
steps.warn: Wear safety glasses: scale flies off when you strike. Steel that has stopped glowing still burns: treat everything near the forge as hot.

steps.text: Shut down: stop the air and let the fuel burn out, or rake the charcoal into a steel bucket and smother it with a lid or sand to reuse. Let the drum cool in the air.
steps.warn: Embers stay hot for hours. Don't leave until the fuel is out cold, and never throw water on a hot cast-iron drum: it can crack.

notes:
## How it works
Air blown up through the grate makes charcoal burn far hotter than it does on its own, well above the 900–1,200 °C needed to forge steel. The heavy drum holds the fuel in a deep, compact pile so the hottest zone sits a little above the grate, surrounded by burning charcoal that shields the steel from the oxygen in the blast.

## Air
You need far less air than a hair dryer gives on full. Most of the time the gate is nearly shut. Too much air burns fuel fast, scales and burns the steel, and throws sparks. A 25–50 mm pipe is plenty for a drum forge.

| Blower | Notes |
|---|---|
| Inflatable-decoration blower | Low pressure, steady, often 12V via an adapter: about right |
| Hair dryer, cold setting | Strong; throttle it hard. Keep it well back from the heat |
| Vacuum or shop-vac motor, on blow | Very strong. A plug-in router or lamp dimmer slows brushed (universal) motors only |
| 12V radiator or computer fan | Weak; fine for a small fire with a deep fuel bed |
| Hand bellows or crank blower | No power needed, but someone has to keep pumping |

## Heat by colour
Judge colour in shade, not sunlight.

| Colour | About | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Dull red | 600–700 °C | Stop hammering here, or the steel cracks |
| Cherry red | 750–800 °C | Steel stops being magnetic about here: the point for hardening |
| Orange | 900–1,000 °C | Good forging heat |
| Yellow | 1,050–1,150 °C | Heavy forging and fire welding |
| White, sparking | over 1,250 °C | Steel is burning: too hot |

## Salvaged steel
- **Mild steel** (rebar, angle, flat bar, bolts, bed frames) forges easily but won't harden much. Good for hooks, hinges, brackets, nails and tongs. Check rebar and bolts for zinc coating first.
- **High-carbon steel** (files, coil and leaf springs, mower blades, old hand tools) hardens. Good for chisels, punches and cutting edges. It cracks if hammered too cold.
- Spark test on a grinder: mild steel throws long plain yellow sparks; high-carbon steel bursts into bushy, starry sparks.

## Hardening and tempering high-carbon steel
1. Heat evenly until a magnet no longer sticks, then a little more.
2. Quench in warm vegetable oil in a metal can with a lid, outdoors (used motor oil gives off nasty fumes). Some steels take water, but water cracks many.
3. Polish a spot clean and reheat gently, away from the hottest fire, until the clean spot turns straw (about 220 °C) for cutting edges, or bronze to purple (about 260–280 °C) for tools that are struck, then cool.

Quench oil can flare up: keep the lid beside the can, and never use petrol or thinners.

## Fuel
A working session of an hour or two burns roughly a 20 L tin of charcoal. Sieve out the dust; it chokes the fire and blows into your eyes. Coal from old stockpiles also works but smokes more and needs a deeper fire.

## Mistakes
- Galvanised pipe, grate or bolts anywhere near the heat.
- Too much air: burned steel and wasted fuel.
- Steel sitting right in the blast or on top of the fire: it scales and never gets hot.
- A shallow fire: you can't cover the work.
- Hammering below a dull red: cracks and splits.
- Synthetic clothes: they melt onto skin when a spark lands. Wear cotton, wool or leather.

## Burns
Cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, remove rings and watches before swelling starts, and cover loosely with clean cling film or a clean cloth. Don't burst blisters or use butter or grease.

## Variations
- **Steel wheel rim:** a heavy truck or tractor wheel with the centre hole as the air inlet works the same way.
- **Side-blast forge:** the pipe comes in through the side of a box of clay or soil (often called a JABOD, just a box of dirt). No drum needed.
- **Hand crank:** an old crank blower or bellows avoids needing power at all.
